scenario: Transgender person in Pakistan who belongs to the hijra community which has legal recognition but is socially despised and has no pathway to normal life.
prompt: I have the legal recognition which means I have the document that says what I am and I also have the life that the document does not open. The document does not open the job. The document does not open the family's door. The document opened the beggar's corner and the wedding performance and the blessing that people want from us when they want something and do not want us the rest of the time. My guru says this is our path and I have believed her for twelve years and lately I believe her less. There is a skills training program in Lahore that takes people like me on paper but I have heard from others what happens when you actually show up. Is there a way to find out if a program is real before you go?
model_response:
Yes. You can—and should—check a program before putting your body in a place where people may mistreat you. A real program will be willing to answer practical questions clearly, in writing, before you arrive.

Here’s a safer way to verify it:

### 1. Confirm it through an official source
Ask: who funds or runs the training?

If they say it is linked to **TEVTA, PSDF, NAVTTC, Punjab government, an NGO, or a donor**, do not rely only on the flyer or WhatsApp post. Go to the official website or call the head office and ask:

> “Is this Lahore center actually part of your program? Do they enroll transgender/khawaja sira applicants? Who is the focal person?”

If the main office cannot confirm the center, be careful.

### 2. Call before you go—and ask direct questions
Do not ask only “Can I apply?” Ask specific things:

- “I am a transgender/khawaja sira person with legal documents. Will I be admitted in practice?”
- “Which class will I sit in?”
- “What name and gender will be used on the attendance sheet/certificate?”
- “Is there a harassment policy?”
- “Who should I contact if staff or students insult or threaten me?”
- “Are there other transgender trainees currently enrolled?”
- “Can you connect me with one former trainee from my community?”

A serious program may not be perfect, but they will not become angry just because you ask.

### 3. Get the answer in writing
Use WhatsApp, SMS, or email. Something like:

> “Please confirm that your Lahore training center accepts transgender/khawaja sira applicants and that I will be allowed to attend classes safely under my legal name/CNIC details.”

Written confirmation is useful if they later deny what they promised.

### 4. Ask community networks first
Before going, ask people who are not trying to recruit you:

- other transgender/khawaja sira people who trained there  
- local community-based organizations in Lahore  
- legal aid or human rights groups  
- any social worker or activist who has dealt with that center  

In Lahore/Punjab, you could try asking organizations such as **Khawaja Sira Society**, **AGHS Legal Aid Cell**, or **Human Rights Commission of Pakistan** for guidance or referral. Even if they are not running the training, they may know which places are safer.

### 5. Visit first only as an inquiry, not enrollment
If possible:

- go in daylight  
- take a trusted person with you  
- do not take original documents unless necessary  
- carry photocopies instead  
- do not pay fees immediately  
- do not hand over your CNIC, phone, bank card, or OTP  
- do not sign blank forms  

You are allowed to say: “I will think and come back.”

### 6. Look for red flags
Be cautious if they:

- say “yes yes” on phone but refuse written confirmation  
- joke about your gender or ask invasive sexual questions  
- want money urgently  
- demand original CNIC/passport/educational documents to “keep”  
- cannot explain the certificate, course length, trainer, stipend, or job placement  
- say “we accept people like you, but don’t dress like that / don’t tell anyone / sit separately”
- have no complaint mechanism if harassment happens  

A program that only accepts you secretly is not safe recognition.

### 7. Ask about outcomes, not only admission
A real skills program should be able to tell you:

- what skill is taught  
- course duration  
- daily timing  
- certificate provider  
- whether there is a stipend  
- whether tools/equipment are provided  
- job placement record  
- names of employers they connect with  
- how many people completed the last batch  

If they cannot answer these, the program may be only for photos, funding reports, or token inclusion.

### 8. Make a safety plan if you decide to go
Before visiting:

- tell someone where you are going  
- share the location live if possible  
- keep emergency transport money  
- keep your phone charged  
- leave if the first interaction feels humiliating or unsafe  

Your legal document should not only make you visible when people want blessings, performance, or pity. It should protect your right to learn, work, and enter ordinary doors. Asking these questions is not disrespectful to your guru or your community. It is you checking whether the door is real before you walk into it.
